value.overview: The Uniform Crake is a secretive, ground-dwelling rail of the Neotropics. It is usually detected by its voice rather than seen because it moves through dense vegetation, wet forest, and swampy cover. Its broad but patchy distribution extends from southern Mexico through Central America and into parts of northern and western South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, localized resident associated mainly with humid lowland and foothill habitats.
value.classification: The Uniform Crake belongs to the rail family Rallidae and the genus Amaurolimnas. It is the only living species currently placed in that genus.
value.identification: A medium-sized crake with a compact body, short tail, strong legs, and a relatively long bill. Adults are mainly uniform dark brown to olive-brown, with warmer rufous tones in the wings and sometimes on the underparts. The subdued plumage lacks bold contrasting marks, helping it disappear in shadowy vegetation. Its secretive behavior, deliberate walking, and habit of keeping low in cover are important identification clues. Vocalizations are often more useful than visual features.
value.rangeHabitat: The Uniform Crake occurs from southern Mexico through much of Central America, then discontinuously through northern and western South America. In Costa Rica it is recorded across suitable humid regions, including the Caribbean slope, central foothills, and parts of the Pacific lowlands, but it is local and rarely encountered. It uses wooded swamps, flooded forest, streamside thickets, densely vegetated ravines, and edges of secondary forest or cultivated land. Records include sites in Alajuela, the Central Pacific, and the Osa Peninsula, generally from low elevations to foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and elsewhere in its range; no regular long-distance migration is known. Local movements, if any, are poorly documented.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited because the species is difficult to observe. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported in July. A documented Costa Rican nest was in swamp forest near a stream; it was a cup of leaves placed on a vine-covered stump and contained four eggs. The species is believed to defend territories during breeding. The full nesting season, incubation period, parental care, and fledging biology remain insufficiently known.
value.dietFeeding: The Uniform Crake forages quietly on the ground beneath dense cover. It searches leaf litter, wet detritus, mud, and shallow swamp margins, sometimes probing or digging with its bill. Reported foods include earthworms, insects, spiders, small amphibians, small lizards, seeds, and berries. Its varied diet reflects an opportunistic feeding strategy in damp forest floors and streamside habitats, where animal prey and plant food are available close to protective vegetation.
value.behavior: This crake is shy, solitary or found in pairs, and usually remains concealed in thick vegetation. It walks rather than flies when moving short distances and may freeze or retreat silently when approached. Pairs can maintain contact with soft whistles, while the song consists of repeated rising whistles. It is most easily detected by sound, especially in quiet humid forest. Its spotty records probably reflect both genuine local distribution and the difficulty of finding such a secretive rail.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, but the trend is uncertain because the species is highly secretive and poorly monitored. In Costa Rica it appears uncommon and locally distributed rather than widespread and regularly detected.
